articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council has agreed to provide child-care at no cost for full-time, in-class Piedmont School District teachers with a need for such service for the remainder of the academic year. “Of the many challenges facing our community during the course of the COVID-19 pandemic, the closure of schools to in-person learning has been one of the hardest,” explained City Administrator Sara Lillevand in a city report. “While many obstacles are beyond our control, [city] staff has examined possible mechanisms the city might undertake to support the [school] district’s efforts to expand in-person learning hours.” Lillevand added that availability and cost of childcare can provide a barrier for educators and staff to return to campuses, and that the city should be able to assist. “The Recreation Department,” she said, “has managed to provide childcare throughout the pandemic and subsequent lockdowns, all in a safe manner and while following guidance directed from the Alameda County Health Department.” The Recreation Department oversees all city childcare programs, including the popular Schoolmates program. The motion, approved unanimously at an April 5 council meeting, authorizes Recreation Director Chelle Putzer to waive childcare fees for employees of the school district who will teach in-person classes for the rest of the 2020 - 21 academic year and a 2021 summer school if it is scheduled. The council will also authorize Putzer to make and enforce rules regarding fee waivers, and requests that the district provide the city with a list of employees who are currently providing on-campus learning and have a need for child care. “Without a full understanding of the needs of Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) employees, the city cannot commit to the feasibility of creating space for all, but it can commit to a good faith effort to expand offerings to meet those needs and to offering programs at no cost,” Lillevand said. Currently, five school district employees have children in Camp Smart Start, the COVID-equivalent of Schoolmates, and have collectively paid $10,000 thus far for the service. The city will commit to supporting this effort without tapping into its general fund, Lillevand explained. A city staff report confirmed that the Schoolmates reserve fund has a current balance of $236,000 and a projected year-end balance of $150,000-$200,000. City staff also expect funds from the American Rescue Plan to be distributed in coming months, which could likely bring one to two million dollars for the city. Support for educators and school staff to return to in-person learning is expected to be an approved expenditure for the funds received.
articles.title: City to provide free childcare for Piedmont teachers

We are writing on behalf of the more than 250 parents in the Advocates for Full-Time, In-Person Piedmont Schools group, as well as the students in the Piedmont Unified School District who have been suffering as a result of distance learning over the past 365+ days. First, we would like to express our sincere gratitude for the many extra hours that all of you have put into our schools throughout this unprecedented year. COVID- 19 has been hard on all of us, but we recognize and appreciate that as educators and administrators, you have experienced a level of stress and exhaustion that many of us cannot fully comprehend. We hear you when you say you are exhausted and burned out. We write to you today because of our respect for what you have taken on, and because of our shared commitment to the students in our district. We are grateful that most Piedmont students now have an opportunity for some in-person instruction. We are also grateful that the district and our local teachers’ union (APT) have reached tentative agreements for expanding secondary in-person class time. We look forward to hearing the details about those new schedules soon. articles.text: 45% of all Piedmont residents fully vaccinated 28.5 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, over 45 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 28 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Even as all adult residents become eligible for vaccination next week, the state expects it will take several months for everyone who wants a vaccine to get one. Last month, Alameda County opened vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years old “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county stated. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. Furthermore, people aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. This week, the county announced that the mass vaccination site at the Oakland Coliseum will remain open even though its contract with FEMA is scheduled to end on Sunday, April 11. The county is still dealing with a demand for vaccine that outstrips supply, although new shipments of doses should mitigate the issue in the coming weeks. The county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 percent of the population. The state has administered about 20.3 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 360,360 people per day, a significant increase compared to last week.

articles.text: Mask mandate required for foreseeable future California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced yesterday, Tuesday, April 6, that the state plans to lift most restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic on June 15. While a mask mandate will stay in place until further notice, Newsom said most restrictions will end if hospitalizations remain low and vaccinations continue apace. “We can confidently say by June 15 that we can start to open up as business as usual, subject to ongoing mask-wearing and ongoing vigilance,” Newsom said at a press conference. “This is a big day,” he added. According to the new plan, California’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy” – the state’s four-tiered color-coded protocol for reopening activities and sectors – will be abolished on June 15. Instead of focusing on specific sectors and industries, the state will focus mostly on masks and vaccinations. Dr. Mark Ghaly, the California Director of Health Services, joined Newsom at the announcement and said there was no timeline for ending the statewide face mask mandate. “We still see masking as a key protective feature,” Ghaly said. Last Tuesday, March 30, the state moved Alameda County into the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier for reopening. As part of the orange tier, the capacity for indoor dining increased to 50 percent and outdoor bars reopened. Gyms and fitness centers reopened at 25 percent capacity, while some indoor offices reopened with modification. Indoor capacity limits for retail were removed. Indoor gatherings are strongly discouraged by the state but are allowed in the orange tier. Only three households can gather at a time with face masks and social distancing. Museums, zoos and family entertainment centers all now have greater indoor capacity. Outdoor live events were permitted beginning Thursday, April 1 with many modifications. Last Friday, April 2, the state announced indoor concerts, performances and other events will be allowed starting next Thursday, April 15. On March 9, Alameda County was moved into the red tier, or substantial tier, the second-most restrictive tier. Before that, the county was in the most-restrictive purple tier, or widespread tier, for several months. The county must meet orange tier benchmarks for at least three weeks before moving into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Accordingly, the soonest the county could move up tiers is April 20. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County remained at 1.4 percent as of Monday, April 5. This rate will need to stay below 4.9 percent for the county to remain in the orange tier. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to stay below 3.9 – right now there are 3.5 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.1 percent in Alameda County. To move into the yellow tier, the cases per day need to be below 1 per 100,000 and the positivity rate needs to be below 2 percent. The positivity rate in low-income census tracts needs to be below 2.2 percent. Two new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont over the past seven days. In total, there have been 172 COVID-19 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 83,979, an increase of 681 new cases week-over-week. There have been 26,074 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,158 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,432 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide, an increase of 31 in the past seven days. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,583,830 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 58,541 deaths due to the disease statewide. In his remarks, Newsom noted that infections are decreasing and that California has “the lowest case rates, positivity rates in America.” California opened COVID- 19 vaccination eligibility last Thursday, April 1 to all people age 50 and over, although vaccination appointments remain in extremely high demand in Alameda County. Expecting an influx of vaccine supply, the state announced last month plans to expand eligibility to all Californians over the age of 16 next Thursday, April 15. Alameda County’s website lists people ages 50 and over as eligible for the vaccine but requests that residents “please complete our notification form to hear when appointments are available.” The notification form is available at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines Californians are also encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. The state asks residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. Three different COVID-19 vaccines are currently being administered in Alameda County. Vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer, mRNA vaccines that were both first approved last year, require two doses injected several weeks apart. A vaccine manufactured by Johnson and Johnson, a viral vector-type vaccine, requires only one dose. Gavin Newsom announced yesterday, Tuesday, April 6, that the state plans to lift most restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic on June 15. While a mask mandate will stay in place until further notice, Newsom said most restrictions will end if hospitalizations remain low and vaccinations continue apace. “We can confidently say by June 15 that we can start to open up as business as usual, subject to ongoing mask-wearing and ongoing vigilance,” Newsom said at a press conference. “This is a big day,” he added. According to the new plan, California’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy” – the state’s four-tiered color-coded protocol for reopening activities and sectors – will be abolished on June 15. Instead of focusing on specific sectors and industries, the state will focus mostly on masks and vaccinations. As part of the orange tier, the capacity for indoor dining increased to 50 percent and outdoor bars reopened. Gyms and fitness centers reopened at 25 percent capacity, while some indoor offices reopened with modification. Indoor capacity limits for retail were removed. Indoor gatherings are strongly discouraged by the state but are allowed in the orange tier. Only three households can gather at a time with face masks and social distancing. Museums, zoos and family entertainment centers all now have greater indoor capacity. Outdoor live events were permitted beginning Thursday, April 1 with many modifications. Last Friday, April 2, the state announced indoor concerts, performances and other events will be allowed starting next Thursday, April 15. On March 9, Alameda County was moved into the red tier, or substantial tier, the second-most restrictive tier. Before that, the county was in the most-restrictive purple tier, or widespread tier, for several months. The county must meet orange tier benchmarks for at least three weeks before moving into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Accordingly, the soonest the county could move up tiers is April 20. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County remained at 1.4 percent as of Monday, April 5. articles.text: MS, OTR/L Are you beginning to think that handwriting is obsolete? This is certainly a valid thought given our students’ dependency over the last year due to the pandemic on keyboarding assignments instead of handwriting them. Keyboarding is always legible and who doesn’t like spell check? At a recent IEP (Individualized Education Plan) meeting for a student that I serve, the topic of handwriting versus keyboarding was raised. Lists can be made on phones, letters sent by email and essays written using Google documents. In short, is handwriting even necessary? To this question, the answer is a resounding Yes. Recent research, comparing handwriting to keyboarding, found handwriting improves memory/recall, comprehension, and even test scores. Handwriting remains an essential skill for both younger and older students, including those in college. Three recent studies noted the following: • Preschool students were taught to copy letters of the alphabet by hand or by typing them. After three weeks of learning, letter recognition tests were completed. The older preschool students in the handwriting instruction/ practice group demonstrated better letter recognition - a fundamental skill for learning letter sounds and reading (Longcamp et al, 2005). • One study compared methods of note taking, handwritten or typed, and the recall and understanding of children 10–11 years old. Using a multiple-choice question (MCQ) format, factual recall and understanding of a history and a biology lesson were assessed. MCQ tests were carried out both immediately after each lesson and one week later. Factual recall was not affected by the note-takStudies show there are many benefits to handwriting, so don’t give up your pencil yet. • ing mode, but those students who wrote their notes by hand had greater conceptual understanding one week after their lesson compared to those who typed notes (Horbury & Edmonds, 2021). Eighty college students were included in a study to compare taking notes or a quiz by hand or on their laptop. Those who took notes by hand performed better on quizzes overall and with conceptual questions than students who took notes on their laptop, suggesting that handwritten notes may improve how students encode and store material. (Crumb et al, 2020). The cognitive benefits of handwriting compared to keyboarding as noted above are just one facet. There are many other benefits from handwriting. Some examples include: • Handwriting helps students to slow down and gather their thoughts. • Handwriting benefits creative writing by removing the urge to immediately edit as one writes thereby allowing thoughts to flow more freely and less fragmented. • Handwriting supports writing outlines and brainstorming ideas. A blank page has no restrictions - add side notes or circle important points to link thoughts. So even though lists can be made on phones, letters sent in an email and essays written on the computer, at a minimum, encourage your student to put down their laptops and take handwritten notes in class, as they read a chapter or make index cards for studying with a nicely sharpened pencil. If your student is a naysayer, share the evidence-based research with them. They may come to realize that they’d prefer an A on that quiz instead of the ease of spell check. Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew, a youth-led coed Venturing unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, is the largest youth volunteer organization of its kind. It actively seeks teen volunteers throughout the year. The crew was founded in 2002 by Ken Li, the Council’s VP of Venturing, who still serves as the Crew Advisor. Li this week was named recipient of Piedmont School District’s annual Volunteer of the Year Award, the Arthur Hecht Award. Under Li’s guidance crew members participate in several ongoing and recurring programs annually. These include tutoring under-served students, making and refurbishing personal protective equipment (PPE), and cooking for essential health workers and for the food insecure. Over its 16-year history, crews have planned and funded the building of the Youth Empowerment Village for Youth Spirit Artworks; designed and constructed planter boxes for Altenheim Retirement Community; and rebuilt an outdoor storage structure for Friends of Causal Creek. This Spring crew members will participate in their largest project of the year, a home restoration project in Oakland that consumes two full weekends. “The project is PCSC’s annual sponsored project with Rebuilding Together Oakland, where youth project leaders select the beneficiary, plan the scope of work and schedule work days that are exclusive to our members,” Li explained. The project was postponed from last spring due to COVID, and is likely to extend into the summer this year, he confirmed. Typically, there are one to two scheduled opportunities a week, as well as programs where members may volunteer from home. Becoming a crew member goes beyond service work by providing a positive environment for youth development and youth leadership, while giving them an opportunity to interact with their peers. PSCS does more than just service; crews have also planned summer service trips, have held teen-organized speaker series, and host awards nights and fundraisers. PSCS exclusively funds and plans the majority of its work. “PCSC fundraising pays for much of the projects that we take on so that the members can be proud of doing much more than just volunteering,” Li said. Adult volunteers are welcomed to join and assist in helping mentor the youth. Parents and adults can sign up for only a few events, or consistently volunteer by completing a BSA signup at https://www.pcservicecrew.org/signup-to-volunteer. New members can visit https://www.pcservicecrew.org/ new-member. articles.text: Last Sunday, April 4th, was Easter. Just like the entire last year, it’s been anything but normal. articles.text: Caroline Devine scored seven goals and had four assists against Monte Vista. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team went toe-to-toe with Monte Vista in Danville before losing 13-12 to the Division 1 North Coast Section opponent. As a reminder, PHS plays in Division 2 and were the 2019 champions. With a shortened season and just five games remaining, and no playoffs planned, coach Carlton Chan was committed to scheduling some solid competition. The Highlanders were well within grasp of a victory, but some confusion on the field took place and mistakenly Monte Vista was awarded an extra possession. The Western Alameda County Conference has new rules for teams with the removal of the draw (faceoff) circle. “We knew we’d play some tough teams. It was a tough loss against Monte Vista. We were doing alternate possessions because of the WACC’s rules against taking draws [faceoffs] and the Mustangs were inadvertently given an extra possession. I can’t blame them because it gets a little confusing with these new rules, but in a 1-score loss, it was critical,” explained Chan. The game was deadlocked at 6-6 going into halftime, and extended to the very last Monte Vista possession for the game-winner. Katherine Kinne got the day started for the Purple and White with a goal in the first 30 seconds, but MV’s Allison Devane followed up with a score of their own after a couple of minutes. Kinne added her second goal to put PHS ahead 2-1, but the Mustangs tied again. “Monte Vista had a couple of strong players, Allison Devane Katherine Kinne (13) scored a hat trick against Monte Vista. was a tough lefty. Who drove well and kicked the ball out perfectly. She always occupied two defenders,” mentioned Chan. The game went back and forth with goals from Caroline Devine, while Sadie Tschider landed a goal on a pass from Devine. While at 4-4, Kinne got her hat trick with 13 minutes left in the half 5-4, but the Mustangs galloped back once again after a minute and a half. Tschider added Piedmont’s sixth goal with around 11 minutes left in the half, but they couldn’t get back on the board with stout defense from both sides. MV’s Devane scored with 6:11 left in the first half and the score remained 6-6 until halftime. The Highlanders jumped into a 2-goal lead right after halftime with scores by Devine and Tschider within five minutes. Some costly turnovers opened the door for the Mustangs to come back. MV got back on the board to make it 8-7 with 20 minutes left, but Devine stretched it back to 9-7—she had the next four scores for PHS, but it unfortunately wasn’t enough. After a Mustang score, Devine scored with 15:20 left in the game on another slick pass from Tschider. The Highlanders held an 11-9 lead with another score from Devine with 11:27 left in the game, but MV stormed back with six goals in the last 10 minutes, and two in the last 30 seconds. Devine scored, once again, with 7:07 on the clock to make it 12-11 and PHS went up 13-11 with slightly over 6 minutes left. But from there, MV’s Jaiden Wire netted their 12th with 3:30 left and the tying goal with 25 seconds on the clock, following a quick turnover at midfield, MV scored the winner. But Devine had one last chance, drawing a foul at the 12-yard line and peeling off an angled shot with 1.2 seconds left after driving past two defenders. Devine, who drew contact within the shooting area, wasn’t given a free-space penalty on the play. “For whatever reason, the refs did not award her free possession and instead placed her on the 12. Even still, she battled through two defenders and the goalie made the save with 1.2 seconds left,” added Chan. Final stats include: Devine with seven goals, four assists. Tschider had three goals, four assists. Kinne scored three goals. Goalie Sophia Ethington recorded three saves in the first half. Lindsay Kottle entered in the second half, recording five saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-4) heads to Berkeley today, Wednesday, April 7, for a 7:00 p.m. match. They play again on Saturday, April 10 at Witter Field against Washington High of Fremont at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: 20-0 shutout win vs. San Lorenzo; 16-6 loss to Mt. Eden Piedmont went from high to low in its last pair of softball games. In a game with two league opponents in the Shoreline Division of the Western Alameda County Conference, PHS demolished San Lorenzo 20-0 at Witter Field in a five-inning game on Monday, April 5. Three days earlier, on Friday, April 2. They were overwhelmed by Mt. Eden 16-6 in Hayward. “You can’t expect any wins in this league. You’ve got to play every game; you could have an off day and end up with a loss,” philosophized PHS coach Gene Diamond. “But we’re starting to see the ball at the plate.” It was another breakout week for sophomore shortstop Leah Bell, who recorded an inside the park home run and a triple against Mt. Eden, and had a triple and two RBI’s against San Lorenzo. “I’ve been feeling pretty good at the plate,” she admitted. “We know that some teams are going to have some faster pitchers, but we’ve beaten these teams before and we can do it again,” said Bell. Despite having only four games left in the season and no WACC playoffs planned, the squad has 12 underclassmen who should return in 2022. Dennard is hopeful their success will lead to more PHS kids trying out. “We’re pretty pleased with where we are after losing the season last season. If we can get everyone back next season, the program will be in a good place and we ‘d like to field a JV team, which I understand hasn’t happened in quite some time,” mentioned Dennard. 20-0 blowout of SLZ The big blowout victory over San Lorenzo featured 14 hits, doubles by Izzy Epstein and Morgan Hunt, a triple by Bell, while Annabel Castronovo pitched a complete five-inning 10-run rule shortened game for five strikeouts and one hit allowed. Sophomore Ginger Gardner notably had seven RBIs on two hits. The Highlanders scored six runs in the bottom of the first inning, four in the second, five in the third, and five more in the fourth inning. Bell got the show started with a leadoff triple and scored on an error during a Castronovo single. After three walks, Castronovo scored and Gretchen Gerhardy hit an RBI single. PHS then scored three runs on an error committed after a hard-hit Ginger Gardner groundball for a 6-0 lead. Starting pitcher Annabel Castronovo recording five strikeouts and one hit allowed over five innings against San Lorenzo. Sophomore Ginger Gardner had seven RBIs with two hits against the Grizzlies.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team split its two games last week, falling to Berkeley 4-0 on the road on Tuesday, March 30, and winning dramatically, 6-5, in a late inning comeback against St. Joseph of Alameda on Saturday, April 3. Sophomore second baseman Michael Aikawa slugged a tworun homerun in the bottom of the sixth to win it for the Highlanders. “All my teammates say that all they saw were fastballs, I think he threw just one off-speed. I was looking for a fastball. I saw a low fastball, inside and low, and turned on it,” explained Aikawa. Aikawa is building quite a resume for his heroics this year. It is his second game-winning hit after smacking an RBI double in an earlier game against Oakland Tech in the bottom of the fifth. But it’s not just Aikawa getting the job done in high-intensity situations. You can label coach Eric Olson’s team the “Clutch Kids.” They have won four of their games by fewer than two runs, and game-winning hits have come in the final two innings. “Unfortunately, we’ve gotten down in some games, but these kids have resolve and a ‘Never Say Die’ attitude,” Olson said. “Give credit to the quality of St. Joe. We’ve come back against some teams who aren’t as good as these guys. It’s one of the best wins I’ve seen here at this diamond,” said Olson after the win at Witter Field. The fire started for Piedmont when down 5-1 entering the bottom of the third inning. They scored progressive runs in the third, fourth, and fifth innings to make it 5-4 St. Joseph. And then Aikawa stepped to the plate in the bottom of the sixth to end it. In the bottom of the third, Aikawa drew a one-out walk and advanced to third base on two wild pitches, scoring on a single by Nico Defazio. Their run in the bottom fourth came after Evan McConathy came around to score after Will Sprague struck a hard line drive to the left fielder to cause a costly error and a 5-3 score. In the bottom of the fifth, Lars Derr reached on an error and came all the way around to score on a hard-hit ball through the infield by Cal Barna, recording a double to bring it within one run, 5-4. He describes having some background with St. Joseph’s pitcher, Emmitt Phinney. “The pitcher is a good friend of me. I knew he’d go fastball with runners on, so I just sat back and ripped it. It was a good at bat; it was fun,” said Barna, who also entered the game as the closing Staff Photo Nico Defazio got the comeback started with an RBI single in the bottom of the third. Staff Photo Cal Barna, who gained the save against St. Joseph, also hit an RBI double in part of PHS’ comeback victory. Photo by Mark Aikawa Michael Aikawa (16) heads to his jubilant teammates at home after hitting a two-run game-winning home run against Berkeley in the bottom of the sixth. pitcher in the top of the seventh. articles.text: She’s “art teacher” to 280 students at Wildwood Elementary School and “mom” to two students at Piedmont Middle School. But Piedmont resident Larraine Seiden is also a working artist whose ability to adapt kept her creating throughout the COVID- 19 pandemic. “I try to harness interruption,” said Seiden, whose work has been seen throughout the Bay Area and across the country. “My time was still the same. I was still teaching the whole time. My kids were here the whole time. I just harnessed that even more — to keep working.” Seiden took inspiration from the new reality that came with the March 2020 shutdown to create several new pieces of art. When the pandemic also forced cancellations of her scheduled art shows and events, she adapted again — and worked with other Piedmont artists to create the 2020 Art Walk. “Everybody here was walking every day,” she said. “I thought, what if we just do an art walk here in town and give people something to see?” “Crowded Room” by Larraine Seiden. Photo by Kristen Hatcher Larraine Seiden in her studio with a work of art from her series “The Vanishing Points Suite.” The concept of artists’ open studio was moved out of doors for almost 20 local artists, who donated a portion of their sales to support arts programs in the local schools. As one of this year’s Piedmont Art Walk participants, Seiden hopes the event will again raise needed funding. “The teachers of the arts really depend on that money and it was harder to get this year,” Seiden said. “We actually had to spend more this year because we had to buy kits for art at home. I had to buy [art supplies] for every student.” Seiden is still managing distance-learning with her Wildwood students and is making plans to exhibit her work over the coming months. Whatever changes the pandemic brings, she will continue to teach and create. “Interruption is just a part of my life,” she said. “I used to fight that, and I just don’t anymore. My art has grown into those interruptions of time.” This year’s Art Walk will take place on Sundey, May 2, from 12 noon to 5 p.m. Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.

articles.text: The 7th Annual Juried Art Show, presented by the Piedmont Center for the Arts, returns to the Center for a juried art exhibition selected from submissions, highlighting a large variety of contemporary 2-dimensional works by Bay Area artists. From a record-high 500 submissions of original art created within the past year, 35 pieces were selected by guest jurors René de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Thanks to an endowment by the family of John P. Thornborrow, cash awards of $4,000 are allocated annually to the top award winners, with an emphasis on honoring emerging artists in the Bay Area. René de Guzman, a Piedmont native and Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, is one of two guest jurors of the 7th Annual Juried Art Show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Exhibition Dates The Juried Art show will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, on weekends from Saturday, April 17 through Sunday, May 16 from 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. each day. COVID Protocols All visitors must sign up in advance for their visit. An emailbased online system will be established where visitors may sign up for their choice of day. A health screening form will be emailed to visitors with their confirmation, also listing all health requirements. Exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Staff will be seated at the entrance, maintaining a roster of visitors correlating to time to facilitate any needed contact tracing, performing temperature checks, and collecting health screening forms. Social distancing norms will be observed while guests visit the exhibition and while waiting to enter, and masks will be worn at all times. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands on entry and to circle the exhibition in a one-way direction to prevent clustering. No food or drink will be permitted. The Center has both a front entrance facing Magnolia and a back door in the North patio. One of these doors will be designated as the sole entrance, and the other as the exit, to avoid two-way traffic through either doorway at any time. articles.text: State releases guidance, reduced restrictions, effective April 1 Woodminster Summer Musicals may be able to return to Woodminster Amphitheater in the Oakland Hills this summer. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and the California Department of Industrial Relations (CAL OSHA) released updated guidance for the safe operation of outdoor, seated, live events and performances. The joint guidance was released on March 26 and went into effect on April 1. According to the guidelines, venues can open for live audiences with a maximum of 33% capacity. Venues may increase attendance capacity to 67% if all guests show a negative test result within 72 hours prior to attendance or show proof of full vaccination. Performers, athletes, and workers who participate in routine, weekly testing are not counted toward any occupancy capacity limit. Only California spectators are to be allowed for outdoor live performances. At the time of ticket purchase, the operator of the venue must obtain verification that the ticket holder lives in California. Only advanced ticket reservations are permissible. These restrictions are in addition to all Center for Disease Control (CDC) sanitation recommendations and employee protocol and training. The 18-page guidance released by the state includes information for various, essential departments in live entertainment, such as casting, set design, scenery, sounds, props, costume and wardrobe and hair and makeup. Performers who “cannot feasibly perform or work with a face covering” (i.e. horn players in music groups) are not required to do so, as long as they are at least six feet from other performers and are routinely tested at least twice weekly for COVID-19. Performers may rehearse indoors. For the purpose of the guidance, a “permissible outdoor venue” is a permanent, fixed facility, either open to the sky with no roof or at least 50% of the perimeter open. It should be designed in a way that provides operators the ability to control the ingress and egress of all visitors; and there must be permanent or added barriers to create at least 12-feet of space between performers and audience members. The guest or ticket holder’s “block” of seat reservations should contain no more than one household, and advance ticketing is required. were released, Alameda County had already moved into the less restrictive Orange Tier, which made more indoor and outdoor business operations possible. Specifically, the guidance provides a loosening of restrictions for live performances, both indoor and outdoor. Nearby outdoor venues Some examples of venues that fit the description are Woodminster Amphitheater, home of the Summer Musical Theatre in Joaquin Miller Park in Oakland, and California Shakespeare Festival, whose summer productions are held at Bruns Amphitheater in the hills near Orinda. Other popular Bay Area music venues such as the Greek Theatre in Berkeley, the Shoreline Amphiteatre in Mountain View, and the Concord Pavilion, would qualify to re-open for outdoor, live events under the new guidance. Woodminster theatre holds 1,200 attendees, and the Bruns Amphitheater holds 545. At 33% capacity, as suggested by state guidelines, Woodminster could hold 396 attendees, and Bruns Amphitheater could hold 179. Woodminster Summer Musicals has not planned for fullstaged performances this summer, but Harriet Schlader, who, with her late husband James Schlader, founded Woodminster Summer Musicals in 1967, said that the company is looking at shows with small casts. Instead of a full orchestra, they will plan to have just a few musicians. Some possible musicals that will grace the stage this summer season include “Mirette,” “I Do, I Do,” “Blood Brothers,” and “Always…Patsy Cline.” Definitive details should be announced soon. Originally scheduled for last summer, 2020, Woodminster will produce An American in Paris, On Your Feet!, and Something Rotten for next year in July, August, and September 2022, respectively.

articles.text: You can now see George Balanchine’s full-length trilogy “Jewels” performed by the San Francisco Ballet and streaming through April 21. Told in three parts ­ – Emeralds, Rubies, and Diamonds – is inspired by the ornate displays at New York City jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels. Emeralds, the first in the trilogy, is set to music by Gabriel Faure. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, April 7, 2021 COVID UPDATE Outdoor, seated live events now permitted State releases guidance, reduced restrictions, effective April 1 Woodminster Summer Musicals may be able to return to Woodminster Amphitheater in the Oakland Hills this summer. By Allyson Aleksey The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and the California Department of Industrial Relations (CAL OSHA) released updated guidance for the safe operation of outdoor, seated, live events and performances. The joint guidance was released on March 26 and went into effect on April 1. According to the guidelines, venues can open for live audiences with a maximum of 33% capacity. Venues may increase attendance capacity to 67% if all guests show a negative test result within 72 hours prior to attendance or show proof of full vaccination. Performers, athletes, and workers who participate in routine, weekly testing are not counted toward any occupancy capacity limit. Only California spectators are to be allowed for outdoor live performances. At the time of ticket purchase, the operator of the venue must obtain verification that the ticket holder lives in California. Only advanced ticket reservations are permissible. These restrictions are in addition to all Center for Disease Control (CDC) sanitation recommendations and employee protocol and training. The 18-page guidance released by the state includes information for various, essential departments in live entertainment, such as casting, set design, scenery, sounds, props, costume and wardrobe and hair and makeup. Performers who “cannot feasibly perform or work with a face covering” (i.e. horn players in music groups) are not required to do so, as long as they are at least six feet from other performers and are routinely tested at least twice weekly for COVID-19. Performers may rehearse indoors. For the purpose of the guidance, a “permissible outdoor venue” is a permanent, fixed facility, either open to the sky with no roof or at least 50% of the perimeter open. It should be designed in a way that provides operators the ability to control the ingress and egress of all visitors; and there must be permanent or added barriers to create at least 12-feet of space between performers and audience members. The guest or ticket holder’s “block” of seat reservations should contain no more than one household, and advance ticketing is required. By the time the guidelines were released, Alameda County had already moved into the less restrictive Orange Tier, which made more indoor and outdoor business operations possible. Specifically, the guidance provides a loosening of restrictions for live performances, both indoor and outdoor. Nearby outdoor venues Some examples of venues that fit the description are Woodminster Amphitheater, home of the Summer Musical Theatre in Joaquin Miller Park in Oakland, and California Shakespeare Festival, whose summer productions are held at Bruns Amphitheater in the hills near Orinda. Other popular Bay Area music venues such as the Greek Theatre in Berkeley, the Shoreline Amphiteatre in Mountain View, and the Concord Pavilion, would qualify to re-open for outdoor, live events under the new guidance. Woodminster theatre holds 1,200 attendees, and the Bruns Amphitheater holds 545. At 33% capacity, as suggested by state guidelines, Woodminster could hold 396 attendees, and Bruns Amphitheater could hold 179. Woodminster Summer Musicals has not planned for fullstaged performances this summer, but Harriet Schlader, who, with her late husband James Schlader, founded Woodminster Summer Musicals in 1967, said that the company is looking at shows with small casts. Instead of a full orchestra, they will plan to have just a few musicians. Some possible musicals that will grace the stage this summer season include “Mirette,” “I Do, I Do,” “Blood Brothers,” and “Always…Patsy Cline.” Definitive details should be announced soon. Originally scheduled for last summer, 2020, Woodminster will produce An American in Paris, On Your Feet!, and Something Rotten for next year in July, August, and September 2022, respectively. articles.text: Aspects of the fabulous career of the Hungarian firebrand violinist Edouard Remenyi. Note the announcement of his final concert in the Orpheum Theater and his notorious “bow of death.” Ever dream a life of romantic adventure? That was the introduction to one of the great radio dramas of the past. They should have done a program on the Hungarian violinist Edouard Remenyi. No one in the entire history of music led a more adventurous life than did Remenyi. He was a firebrand revolutionary in the 1848 Hungarian revolution. He fled Europe under penalty of death, came to the United States when our country was really wild, and played in the gold mining towns. Every music lover knows Brahms‘ Hungarian dances. So, let me ask you; who wrote Brahms’ Hungarian dances? Wrong. It was not Brahms at all. He plagiarized them… all of them. You need to remember that Brahms was a cocktail lounge piano player from the north of Germany; very far removed musically and culturally from the Hungarian gypsies. The composer was none other than Edouard Remenyi, that Hungarian firebrand. But now to return to our story. Remenyi was born in Hungary and had the usual musical education in Vienna. He was a child prodigy. And now the story gets really interesting. 1848 was the year of revolution everywhere. The Hungarians revolted against the young Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph. General Kossuth, the leader of the Hungarians in revolt, chose Remenyi to be the psychological leader of the revolution. The young violinist played his violin in every military camp, drumming up enthusiasm. After Emperor Franz Joseph put down the revolution, he placed a bounty on Remenyi – “wanted dead or alive.“ Remenyi fled for his life as far from Europe as he could go. He came all the way to America and became an instant success. He traveled throughout the entire country playing concerts in formal concert halls as well as in saloons in the Wild West. Sometimes the miners were so enthusiastic that they threw gold nuggets onto the stage. On another occasion, Remenyi was so fatigued, he could not play the numerous encores the audience wanted. That’s when Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph changed his mind. You guessed it. Franz Josef wanted Remenyi to be his private violinist in Vienna. It seems that all was forgiven. articles.text: The Telegraph Quartet will give a virtual performance on Sunday, April 18, presented by Crowden Music Center as part of its “Sundays at Four” concert series. The quartet is comprised of Eric Chin and Joseph Maile (violins), Pei-Ling Lin (viola), and Jeremiah Shaw (cello). The performance will feature Britten’s Three Divertimenti; Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 1 in F Major, Op. 18 No. 1; and Brahms’ String Quartet No. 2 in A minor, Op. 51 No. 2. The concert will be performed and streamed live and is free to watch online with advance reservations; it will also be available for on-demand viewing for one week following the livestream on April 18. “All three of these works represent each composer’s first public foray into the string quartet medium,” explained Maile. “Benjamin Britten’s spirited Three Divertimenti were some of the young composer’s first professional works. Beethoven’s Op. 18 No. 1 is his ambitious, if slightly delayed, entry into the quartet medium as the vanguard of his set of six quartets. And Brahms’ wistful second string quartet is one of his two final products, of numerous discarded attempts – most likely with Beethoven metaphorically looking over his shoulder.” The concert will begin at 4 p.m. To reserve tickets, visit https://www.crowden.org/telegraph-quartet.

articles.text: Mary Elizabeth Winstead and John Goodman in 10 Cloverfield Lane. Review by Chris Honore’ If you move in the right creepy-movie circles, you may have seen the 2008 film Cloverfield, a found camcorder style movie about a monster rampaging through Manhattan. But if you didn’t, no worries. 10 Cloverfield Lane is not a sequel, but a standalone taut psychological thriller that does have a high creep factor, but is far more subtle though unsettling than its distant cousin. The use of “Cloverfield” in the title is just good marketing. If there is a fragile thread that connects the two, it runs through J. J. Abrams (“The Force Awakens”), a guy who knows a good story when he finds one. This is indeed a sinister tale that makes superb use of what might be referred to as the “terror-trope.” If all of this is beginning to feel like I’m avoiding even hinting at the plot, you’d be right. The less you know about what to expect from 10 Cloverfield Lane, the better. Try not to watch the trailer. What you will experience going in is a master class in pacing and ambience, using those enjoyably uncomfortable yet familiar emotions such as claustrophobia and paranoia. Meanwhile you will be doing your own check regarding what is real and what are the demented delusions of a wacked-out survivalist. That would be the talented John Goodman as a guy named Howard. Without giving too much away, this is what you might call a container film – a hothouse of riveting tension, created by the fact that the situation is inescapable. This story takes place in an underground bunker that offers as many amenities as can be created, all predicated on not going topside for one to two years. Whatever’s up there, Howard insists, he doesn’t want to experience. The three actors are excellent, led by a solid and nuanced performance by Goodman and buttressed by a convincing, resourceful, McGuyver-like damsel-in-distress portrayal by Mary Elizabeth Winstead as Michelle. The third corner of the triangle is John Gallagher Jr., a local handyman called Emmett, who talked his way into the bunker. Winstead didn’t. Whether you agree with the film’s ending or not will be a personal judgment. It may satisfy or it may be simply too predictable. Admittedly, the writers do get themselves into a bit of a jam, though the story possess that wonderful, chilling, sustained sense of dread. Which is exactly the emotion – call it that affective thriller sweet spot – that films of this genre aim for. Nailed. 10 Cloverfield Lane. Directed by Dan Trachtenberg. Starring John Goodman, Mary Elizabeth Winstead and John Gallagher. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: 10 Cloverfield Lane a scary thriller for everyone

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Free State of Jones brings to the screen a little-known moment taken from the pages of America’s Civil War. The year is 1863. A poor southern Mississippi farmer, Newton Knight (Matthew McConaughey), having deserted his post as a front-line nurse, brings the body of his nephew back to Jones County for burial. He is told repeatedly by his neighbors that Confederate agents are confiscating farmers’ livestock, grain and goods for the war effort. Hearing these stories Newton has an epiphany: what he and his brethren are fighting for is the right of the rich plantation owners to continue to grow cotton and own slaves (of which he has neither). And thus begins the first stirring of what will soon grow into an armed rebellion of runaway slaves and a band of Confederate deserters who soon are fighting a war within a war, deciding they’d prefer to cast their lot with the Union. Writer/director Gary Ross (Sea Biscuit, Hunger Games) wades into this chapter in our history knowing that it is a labyrinth of complexity and nuance. It is a project he had contemplated for almost a decade. He shows remarkable restraint when demonstrating that while the poor whites of Mississippi do not bear the weight and cruelty of racism, they are, like the slaves of the south, disenfranchised. And so, Newton and his ragtag company of slaves and runaway Confederate soldiers begin a guerilla campaign against the soldiers of the South, against its privileged aristocracy, establishing what came to be known as the Free State of Jones, a piece of geography they managed to hold until the end of the war. Free State of Jones represents the nexus of economic and racial oppression. The film is a stark reminder of the inhumanity and profound cruelty of an institution that still astonishes and ripples through our society. Before the Civil War was a time when black lives mattered for their free labor. The value of slaves was solely an economic process, never a human one. But this film is not about a “white savior” helping the oppressed. Newton joins forces not just with those white men who’ve deserted, but he finds a boon companion in Moses Washington (Mahershala Ali), a runaway slave who displays as deep well of intelligence and courage as does Newton. He is also helped by and attracted to Rachel (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), a household slave, who joins him in purpose and in emotional attachment. This band of black brothers and sisters is as essential to Newton’s victory as are the white soldiers who, especially after Vicksburg, decide to take up arms against the South. Free State of Jones is not a perfect film. Ross wanted to tell a story that easily could have been Jones plus a sequel, one in which he dealt with Jim Crow and Plessy v, Ferguson. The Civil War did not end racial prejudice; it just altered its posture. Regardless of the criticism that Free State of Jones is too long, what Ross has accomplished with this story is remarkable, a tale of courage and rebellion and one that we should never forget. Free State of Jones. Starring Matthew McConaughey, Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Mahershala Ali. Directed by Gary Ross. 2 hrs., 19 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Free State of Jones a little-known chapter from the Civil War

Free State of Jones a little-known chapter from the Civil War Review by Chris Honoré Free State of Jones brings to the screen a little-known moment taken from the pages of America’s Civil War. The year is 1863. A poor southern Mississippi farmer, Newton Knight (Matthew McConaughey), having deserted his post as a front-line nurse, brings the body of his nephew back to Jones County for burial. He is told repeatedly by his neighbors that Confederate agents are confiscating farmers’ livestock, grain and goods for the war effort. Hearing these stories Newton has an epiphany: what he and his brethren are fighting for is the right of the rich plantation owners to continue to grow cotton and own slaves (of which he has neither). And thus begins the first stirring of what will soon grow into an armed rebellion of runaway slaves and a band of Confederate deserters who soon are fighting a war within a war, deciding they’d prefer to cast their lot with the Union. Writer/director Gary Ross (Sea Biscuit, Hunger Games) wades into this chapter in our history knowing that it is a labyrinth of complexity and nuance. It is a project he had contemplated for almost a decade. He shows remarkable restraint when demonstrating that while the poor whites of Mississippi do not bear the weight and cruelty of racism, they are, like the slaves of the south, disenfranchised. And so, Newton and his ragtag company of slaves and runaway Confederate soldiers begin a guerilla campaign against the soldiers of the South, against its privileged aristocracy, establishing what came to be known as the Free State of Jones, a piece of geography they managed to hold until the end of the war. Free State of Jones represents the nexus of economic and racial oppression. The film is a stark reminder of the inhumanity and profound cruelty of an institution that still astonishes and ripples through our society. Before the Civil War was a time when black lives mattered for their free labor. The value of slaves was solely an economic process, never a human one. But this film is not about a “white savior” helping the oppressed. Newton joins forces not just with those white men who’ve deserted, but he finds a boon companion in Moses Washington (Mahershala Ali), a runaway slave who displays as deep well of intelligence and courage as does Newton. He is also helped by and attracted to Rachel (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), a household slave, who joins him in purpose and in emotional attachment. This band of black brothers and sisters is as essential to Newton’s victory as are the white soldiers who, especially after Vicksburg, decide to take up arms against the South. Free State of Jones is not a perfect film. Ross wanted to tell a story that easily could have been Jones plus a sequel, one in which he dealt with Jim Crow and Plessy v, Ferguson. The Civil War did not end racial prejudice; it just altered its posture. Regardless of the criticism that Free State of Jones is too long, what Ross has accomplished with this story is remarkable, a tale of courage and rebellion and one that we should never forget. Free State of Jones. Starring Matthew McConaughey, Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Mahershala Ali. Directed by Gary Ross. 2 hrs., 19 min. Rated R. Democracy is not a spectator sport! Onward is a release by Pixar-Disney in which they once again bring to bear what is a marvelous engine of imagination that creates, with each film, a special world that beckons kids of all ages to enter and enjoy. The world created in Onward is one of blue-toned elves who live in toadstool houses, a place of dragons, unicorns, magic spells, and not to forget some engaging wizardry. From the outset the story is carried by two brothers, Ian (Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and Barley (Chris Pratt), older and just a tad different and rebellious. They are the Lightfoot bros, and a study in contrast. They discover a birthday gift left for Ian by his deceased dad: it’s a wizard’s staff along with a letter of instructions that will allow their dad to return for just one day. Ian, with Barley’s help, makes a valiant attempt, but only manages to get halfway through the spell, resulting in dad ending up as a pair of pants, socks and shoes. What is needed is a new gemstone to replace the one that fizzled. Barley is certain he knows where to find one. And so, the adventure begins. The brothers set out on a quest that will take them from place to place, each fraught with perilous moments. The part of this hunt that is unusual is that they take half their dad along, hooked up to a doggy leash so he can’t wander off. Dad, after all, can’t speak or see hence is high maintenance. Their mode of transportation is Barley’s well-used van, outfitted with some amazing stuff, like blasting air conditioning. The boys bicker about directions and the ability of Ian to use the staff to create critical magic when needed – like a magical bridge. What is surprising is that there is a tone of sadness to the story. Both the brothers are grieving for their dad. Ian never knew his father, since he was born shortly after dad died. Barley, however, does have small kid memories and yearns for more. They are convinced that once they locate the special stone they can complete their dad’s final transformation and have that one conversation. And so, onward. The film is essentially episodic and situational, and there are lots of speed bumps along the way. And for good measure, mom Laurel (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) is right behind the pair, desperate to find them, certain they are in danger. It’s all in the Pixar wheelhouse, and kids, say six and seven, will enjoy the journey and the cast of characters, including Colt-Bronco, a police officer centaur (Mel Rodriquez), and a Manticore restaurant with a Manticore (Octavia Spencer). It’s where they find a needed map to get them from point A to point B. It’s all a trip to be enjoyed, especially if you’re a kid and relish quality time in elf-land. Onward. Directed by Dan Scanlon. Animated. With voices of Chris Pratt, Tom Holland, Octavia Spencer and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: It’s been some 25 years since the first Jurassic Park was released, directed by Steven Spielberg, based on the Michael Crichton book, the central idea being that cretaceous creatures, most especially the high-rise dinosaurs with those signature reptilian eyes, could be reproduced using engineered DNA. It was a massive hit that combined all the ingredients of horror and action filmmaking for a breathtaking experience. As well, there is a through line from, say, a film like Jaws to the Jurassic series where a predator is loose and humans, no matter how resilient or well-defended, are ultimately helpless. A sense of overwhelming vulnerability represents the genius of these stories. After all, teethfilled jaws come in all sizes and the image of a person’s torso dangling part way out of a raptor’s mouth will cause viewers to pay attention. Each of the movies that have followed, in the aggregate, have created what has been a durable franchise, while giving audiences a rush of adrenalin as computer generated raptors, scarily smart, manage to get free and overcome all best efforts to contain them. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom, is the second in what will be a trilogy that began with Jurassic World. The set-up is fairly straightforward. The island of Isla Nublar was devastated when the dinos got loose. What made World riveting was that the island is now a popular amusement park, all revolving around the reptiles. The dinos, now free, devastate the park and the tourists, who run for their lives. Finally the island is abandoned to the animals. What has now occurred in Fallen Kingdom is that a once dormant volcano is on the cusp of erupting and Claire (Bryce Dallas Howard) and Owen (Chris Pratt) are recruited by a long-ago benefactor, Benjamin Lockwood (James Cromwell), to rescue the remaining dinos and transport them to another island absent tourists and rides. But, as is explained, the plan, born of avarice, is orchestrated by a nefarious Lockwood assistant unbeknownst to Lockwood. The plan is to put the captured dinos on the market to the highest bidder. So, instead of a pristine island, they are sent to the Lockwood compound, a massive, 19th century manor house. Claire, Owen, and their two aids, Zia (Daniella Pineadad) and Franklin (Justice Smith), manage to sneak onto a boat along with the animals. The exit from the island entails scenes of the island exploding as well as a harrowing trip to the Lockwood home, a darkly gothic warren of spaces with a basement filled with cages where the dinos are kept until auctioned off. Assume that at the manor what can go wrong will go wrong, only the location is no longer an island, but a dark, atmospheric, three-story house with a firstfloor entry replete with museum quality dioramas of dinos in their prehistoric habitats. The dilemma facing Claire, Owen, and sidekicks, is how to rescue the dinos, thus preventing them from falling into the commercial hands of potential buyers. Think raptors weaponized. Things, however, go from dicey to very bad. What has always been a strength of this franchise is that there have been tweens or teens woven into the plot. And Kingdom is no exception. Lockwood, so it seems, has a teenage granddaughter, Maisie (Isabella Sermon), who is terrified. One of the best scenes that kids will definitely relate to is when Maisie, hiding under her covers with an Indoraptor (a designer raptor) standing over her bed, a long claw tapping the tile floor. It’s a chilling moment. When I screen any of the Jurassic films, I remind myself that the audience is made up of youngsters. They show up to be scared and the challenge is always how to go about creating that creepy, terrifying feeling in all its variations. Discussing this point in an email exchange with Piedmont native and co-writer, Colin Trevorrow, the director of Jurassic World, he wrote: “We have a responsibility to appeal to everyone around the world. These movies don’t belong to America, they’re global, and they need to incorporate universal themes that can connect with a hugely diverse audience. It’s not just about age. It’s diversity of experience, of context. Many movies have the luxury of appealing to one group. We have to think about everybody.” Kingdom is a bridge movie and the second in the Jurassic World trilogy. Much of what takes place is leading to the final film. As Trevorrow wrote, “We can’t get to where we’re going without this…. The dynamic between the characters has completely shifted by the end of this story. The equilibrium of the planet has been altered. Nothing will ever be the same for them, or the world they live in.” The challenge, of course, will be how to make the third story fresh and compelling. But then the films that followed Jurassic Park were never about the big reveal. As mentioned, it’s about exploring the dimensions of vulnerability. Recall in Jaws the young woman taking a late-night swim while just below is the ultimate predator, pacing her in what she assumes are benign waters. And there was, of course, that brilliant, memorable soundtrack. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Directed by J.A. Bayona. Written by Colin Trevorrow and Derek Connelly. Starring Chris Pratt, Bryce Dallas Howard and Rafe Spall. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: If people know of Marsala wine at all, it is likely they remember buying a bottle for five bucks about 10 years ago to make chicken Marsala, and the bottle still sits in the cupboard. Let me give you a little historical background before we talk about the wine itself. Marsala is a fortified wine, dry or sweet, produced in the region surrounding the city of Marsala in Sicily. It was probably first popularized outside Sicily by the English trader John Woodhouse. In 1773, he landed at the port of Marsala and discovered the local wine produced in the region, which was aged in wooden casks and tasted similar to Spanish and Portuguese fortified wines then popular in England. Fortified Marsala was, and is, made using a process called in perpetuum, which is similar to the solera system used to produce Sherry in Jerez, Spain. Woodhouse recognized that the in perpetuum process raised the alcohol level and alcoholic taste of this wine while also preserving these characteristics during long-distance sea travel. Woodhouse further believed that fortified Marsala would be popular in England. The wine indeed proved so successful that Woodhouse returned to Sicily and, in 1796, began its mass production and commercialization. Popularity grew over the years. Slightly less than 200 years later, in 1969, Marsala received its DOC status as a protected name from the European Union. Marsala wine is frequently used in cooking and is especially prevalent in Italian food. Dry Marsala is used in savory cooking. A typical savory Marsala sauce, for example, involves reducing the wine almost to a syrup with onions or shallots, then adding mushrooms and herbs. The ever-popular dinner of Chicken Marsala is flour-coated pounded chicken breast halves braised in a mixture of Marsala, butter, olive oil, mushrooms and spices. Sweet Marsala is used to produce rich Italian desserts such as zabaglione and tiramisu. The following wines are excellent examples of both dry and sweet styles of Marsala. • 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry This delicious Sicilian wine is amber colored with aromas and notes of toffee, nuts, raisins and other dried fruits. It is rich and yet not ponderous or cloying with good acid and structure. It can be served chilled as an aperitif or sipped at room temperature after dinner. 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry. • 2017 Cantina Florio Vecchioflorio Marsala Superiore Sweet This sweet Marsala is aged 24 months in oak casks and is mellow as can be. It has a dark amber color with an intense aroma with hints of dates and peaches. On the palate it is deep and rich with a long satisfying finish. An excellent post-prandial dram. Pierre’s Cocktail – an Extra Bonus In addition to being a wine man, at times I dabble a bit in mixology. So these two wines inspired me to see if I could come up with a cocktail that did these hedonistic wines justice. So here it is. DUMONT’S DOWNFALL • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Dry Marsala • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Sweet Marsala • 1 oz. Dry Curacao • 2 dash Angostura Bitters Stir gently with ice then pour over ice into an old-fashioned glass. Garnish with a slice of orange. DuMont’s Downfall – a cocktail combining both dry and sweet Marsala.

articles.text: Every spring I eagerly anticipate the arrival of strawberries at my favorite farmers market vendors. It takes a lot of restraint to skip them the first couple of weeks when they look under ripe with white shoulders and ruby tips. Perhaps the farmers are as eager as the rest of us to see a new season dawning for fruit varieties. But by early April I dive in. Our younger son always requests Strawberry Shortcake for his early-April birthday dessert. So, no matter their ripeness, I’m heading home with two or three baskets. They always look delicious, but it’s clear their flavor has not quite caught up to peak strawberry-liciousness. Adding them to a salad does not disappoint though. The additional ingredients and dressing help to amplify the strawberry flavor, and they are still stunning to the eye. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department has announced that the Walking on Wednesdays group, sidelined for one year due to the coronavirus, will be back in action next Wednesday, April 14. This restart marks three years since the group’s first weekly walk on April 18, 2018. Some new protocols will help keep walkers as COVID-safe as possible. Before the pandemic, many people enjoyed the weekly Wednesday morning walks on Piedmont’s beautiful streets. “Members of the group have remained in contact during the pandemic. Being able to be with members of the group again will be great,” said coordinator Dick Carter. Since last week, March 30, Alameda County has been at the Orange Tier level within the state’s Blueprint for Safer Economy Opening Plan. The Orange Tier allows for many outdoor group activities to be conducted. Individuals planning on participating in the weekly walks need to register on the Recreation Department’s CommunityPass site. pages.text: Wednesday, April 7, 2021 23 The Wine Corner The Magic of Marsala By Pierre DuMont If people know of Marsala wine at all, it is likely they remember buying a bottle for five bucks about 10 years ago to make chicken Marsala, and the bottle still sits in the cupboard. Let me give you a little historical background before we talk about the wine itself. Marsala is a fortified wine, dry or sweet, produced in the region surrounding the city of Marsala in Sicily. It was probably first popularized outside Sicily by the English trader John Woodhouse. In 1773, he landed at the port of Marsala and discovered the local wine produced in the region, which was aged in wooden casks and tasted similar to Spanish and Portuguese fortified wines then popular in England. Fortified Marsala was, and is, made using a process called in perpetuum, which is similar to the solera system used to produce Sherry in Jerez, Spain. Woodhouse recognized that the in perpetuum process raised the alcohol level and alcoholic taste of this wine while also preserving these characteristics during long-distance sea travel. Woodhouse further believed that fortified Marsala would be popular in England. The wine indeed proved so successful that Woodhouse returned to Sicily and, in 1796, began its mass production and commercialization. Popularity grew over the years. Slightly less than 200 years later, in 1969, Marsala received its DOC status as a protected name from the European Union. Marsala wine is frequently used in cooking and is especially prevalent in Italian food. Dry Marsala is used in savory cooking. A typical savory Marsala sauce, for example, involves reducing the wine almost to a syrup with onions or shallots, then adding mushrooms and herbs. The ever-popular dinner of Chicken Marsala is flour-coated pounded chicken breast halves braised in a mixture of Marsala, butter, olive oil, mushrooms and spices. Sweet Marsala is used to produce rich Italian desserts such as zabaglione and tiramisu. The following wines are excellent examples of both dry and sweet styles of Marsala. • 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry This delicious Sicilian wine is amber colored with aromas and notes of toffee, nuts, raisins and other dried fruits. It is rich and yet not ponderous or cloying with good acid and structure. It can be served chilled as an aperitif or sipped at room temperature after dinner. 2015 Cantina Florio Vecchiflorio Marsala Superiore Dry. • 2017 Cantina Florio Vecchioflorio Marsala Superiore Sweet This sweet Marsala is aged 24 months in oak casks and is mellow as can be. It has a dark amber color with an intense aroma with hints of dates and peaches. On the palate it is deep and rich with a long satisfying finish. An excellent post-prandial dram. Pierre’s Cocktail – an Extra Bonus In addition to being a wine man, at times I dabble a bit in mixology. So these two wines inspired me to see if I could come up with a cocktail that did these hedonistic wines justice. So here it is. DUMONT’S DOWNFALL • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Dry Marsala • 1 oz. Cantina Florio Sweet Marsala • 1 oz. Dry Curacao • 2 dash Angostura Bitters Stir gently with ice then pour over ice into an old-fashioned glass. Garnish with a slice of orange. DuMont’s Downfall – a cocktail combining both dry and sweet Marsala. It takes a lot of restraint to skip them the first couple of weeks when they look under ripe with white shoulders and ruby tips. Perhaps the farmers are as eager as the rest of us to see a new season dawning for fruit varieties. But by early April I dive in. Our younger son always requests Strawberry Shortcake for his early-April birthday dessert. So, no matter their ripeness, I’m heading home with two or three baskets. They always look delicious, but it’s clear their flavor has not quite caught up to peak strawberry-liciousness. Adding them to a salad does not disappoint though. The additional ingredients and dressing help to amplify the strawberry flavor, and they are still stunning to the eye. I chose kale as the primary green as we always seem to have a bunch of kale ready to go. This springtime salad is a perfect use, but any leafy green such as spinach, arugula, or lettuce will be tasty too. A few notes: If the kale is a bit tough, you may have to massage it with a small amount of the dressing to help soften it. Even though I chose a curly red for the photos, I often use lacinato kale as it is often more tender. Slicing the kale thinly, across the ribs, helps too. This recipe is adaptable in many ways. Add in cheese, avocado, switch out the pecans for toasted sliced almonds. Go with what you like. Side note: Omit the honey in the dressing and try it on steamed new potatoes with snap peas. INGREDIENTS • 1 bunch kale, either torn or sliced into 1/2-inch wide strips • 1 pint fresh strawberries, sliced lengthwise in halves or thirds, depending on size • 1/2 small red onion, sliced thinly and crosswise to create rings • 1/2 cup pecan pieces, lightly toasted • 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil • 2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice, use sweeter Meyer lemons if available • 1/4 cup loosely packed, fresh mint leaves, finely minced • 1 teaspoon honey, optional, to taste • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Make the dressing: Measure the lemon juice into a small, deep bowl. Add honey, if using. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil, whisking continuously to maximize emulsification. Add minced mint leaves, salt, and pepper to taste. Set aside. Rinse the leaves of kale to remove any dirt and dry well. Either tear into bite-sized pieces, or slice into 1/ 2”-wide strips. Place into a large salad bowl. Pour about half of the prepared dressing over the kale and mix well to begin softening the kale. Add the sliced red onion, toss to mix, then drizzle in additional dressing to taste – taking care to avoid drowning the salad with too much. Add the sliced strawberries and gently combine. Finally, sprinkle on the toasted pecan pieces and serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: The Oakland Public Library (OPL) will open 16 locations including the Piedmont Avenue Branch for indoor Express services starting April 19. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. In 1913, he gathered several successful Piedmont businessmen to purchase land opposite Piedmont Park, and hired Albert Farr to design the Piedmont Commercial Center, the first stores in Piedmont. The primary focus of this adventure will be on whisky tasting and studying the subtleties of peat and esters. The kickoff to this hard-nosing jaunt came in London, where the emphasis was on gins. Because, well, when in Rome, as they say. Tucked away on an easily missed side alley of Fleet Street is the City of London Distillery. Founded in 2012, the urban upstart is bringing back the tradition of gin distillation to the City of London after a nearly 200-year absence. During the eighteenth century, gin distilleries sprouted in this area, originally the site of a fortified Roman settlement at Londonium, as citrus fruits became available through London’s port. Among the distillery’s gins, The Square Mile is a nod to the two square miles that establishes the City of London as a separate entity, complete with its own mayor and independent police force, within the jurisdiction of Greater London. Its doorway sits beneath the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and the press. Down the narrow wooden stairs is the bottle shop, bar, tasting room, and fireproofed, glassed-walled distillery. The cozy setup, complete with dark green paint and plush leather chairs, echoes an era when cigarette smoke might have lingered overhead and the din of clacking typewriters would have overridden conversation (perhaps of the latest news tip?). It’s one-part speakeasy to two-parts journalist hideaway. Jake meets me to host a tour – including the botanicals room, where guests can tinker with their own blends of spices and take the concoction home – and a tasting. The four pillars of the City of London production line are all in the classic London Dry style, with varying levels of citrus. In 2016, the Christopher Wren, named for the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral, the more recognizable church-top to overlook the distillery, took home the same award. Where the Christopher Wren carries more undertones of orange, the citrus lacing the Old Tom is primarily lemon zest. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org.

articles.text: Six juveniles in a stolen vehicle with a concealed handgun were arrested and sent to Juvenile Hall on Saturday, March 27 by Piedmont Police officers. At 7:26 p.m. the Automatic License Plate Reader recorded a hit on a stolen blue 1999 Lexus RX300 SUV heading north on Estates Drive near Park Boulevard. The vehicle was reported stolen and had been used in a carjacking in Oakland three days earlier. Piedmont Officers responded to the scene, located the vehicle at a dead-end near Sunnyhills Road and Downey Place, and initiated a vehicle stop. Four juveniles were initially detained in the front and rear seats of the car. A search of the vehicle found two more juveniles laying down in the back trunk portion of the SUV. A further search of the vehicle revealed credit cards and ID cards in names of other people, and a 9mm semi-automatic handgun. With the assistance of Oakland Police, Piedmont officers arrested all six individuals and transported them to the Police station. The juveniles were booked into Juvenile Hall without incident on charges of Stolen Vehicle, Armed Carjacking, Possession of Stolen Property, and Possession of a Concealed Firearm. One suspect also had an active warrant for his arrest.

CRIME REPORT Police arrest 6 juveniles for carjacking, concealed weapons By Jay Russell Six juveniles in a stolen vehicle with a concealed handgun were arrested and sent to Juvenile Hall on Saturday, March 27 by Piedmont Police officers. At 7:26 p.m. the Automatic License Plate Reader recorded a hit on a stolen blue 1999 Lexus RX300 SUV heading north on Estates Drive near Park Boulevard. The vehicle was reported stolen and had been used in a carjacking in Oakland three days earlier. Piedmont Officers responded to the scene, located the vehicle at a dead-end near Sunnyhills Road and Downey Place, and initiated a vehicle stop. Four juveniles were initially detained in the front and rear seats of the car. A search of the vehicle found two more juveniles laying down in the back trunk portion of the SUV. A further search of the vehicle revealed credit cards and ID cards in names of other people, and a 9mm semi-automatic handgun. With the assistance of Oakland Police, Piedmont officers arrested all six individuals and transported them to the Police station. The juveniles were booked into Juvenile Hall without incident on charges of Stolen Vehicle, Armed Carjacking, Possession of Stolen Property, and Possession of a Concealed Firearm.
